I tucked my notebook into my bag and stepped out into the soft hiss of evening rain. The city air smelled like wet stone and distant thunder, carrying memories I’d tried to leave behind. Some days, the past lingers like an old bruise—faint but always there, reminding you of how tender you once were.

A café’s warm glow spilled onto the cobblestone street. I hesitated outside, watching steam curl from a stranger’s coffee cup. Inside, an elderly woman strummed a guitar in the corner, her fingers dancing over the strings with surprising grace. No one paid her much mind; they were too busy scrolling, typing, rushing from one digital screen to the next. I wished I could tell them to look up. To *feel* the weight of the rain on their skin, the scratch of paper under their fingers, the ache of silence you only find when you let the world slow down.

But I didn’t. Instead, I ordered tea and sat by the window, watching the rain blur the neon signs into streaks of color. It wasn’t just the weather that shifted things—time did, too. Grief, joy, love, all of it folded into the quiet rhythm of breathing.

As I left, I let a loose page from my notebook drift to the floor. The wind would take it eventually. Maybe someone would find it—tuck it back into their own thoughts. Maybe not. But the act itself felt like surrendering to the unknown, letting life write its own messy, beautiful chapters without me insisting on holding the pen.
